children: A parliamentary committee proposed diluting capital demands for UBS by allowing the $170 bln bank to use cheaper additional Tier 1 debt. The same lawmakers want these hybrid securities to be more useful in a crisis. Judging by Credit Suisse’s collapse, the reforms fail that test.
Full view will be published shortly.
Follow Liam Proud on Bluesky and LinkedIn.
Swiss Finance Minister Karin Keller-Sutter on September 1 criticised a parliamentary committee's proposal to soften stricter capital rules proposed by the government for UBS.

Keller-Sutter and the country's financial regulators want the bank to fully capitalise its foreign units in the future, solely using 100% Common Equity Tier 1 capital, the highest quality form of equity, in a step that would raise the lender's overall requirements by about $20 billion.

But the parliamentary committee, citing competitiveness concerns, passed an amended version of the draft legislation stipulating that UBS could back the units with 50% CET1 capital and 50% Additional Tier 1 capital. The latter are hybrid debt securities that can convert into equity if required to help stabilise a troubled bank.

"It does not improve the situation, quite the opposite," Keller-Sutter said, noting that experts from the Swiss National Bank and market regulator FINMA felt the committee's proposal created legal uncertainty and was impractical.
UBS, meanwhile, said on September 1 that the new proposals would still require it to hold about $13 billion in extra Tier 1 capital.
